newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Belgrade bourse readies for increased equity trade.
newsitem.headline: Belgrade bourse readies for increased equity trade.

text.p: The Belgrade Stock Exchange (BSE), which currently trades mostly in short-term debentures, said on Monday it was actively preparing for expected privatisation in the country.
"We are seriously preparing for coming privatisation which will contribute to our business by creating a domestic capital market," Pava Zecevic, the BSE director, told Reuters.
"Although the BSE is not included in the first phase of the ownership transformation, logistically we must do a lot to be ready to absorb and deal with increased needs for trade."
The privatisation law, expected to be passed by the Serbian parliament in coming days, is to take effect in October.
The law falls short of voucher privatisation involving the public as a whole but relies heavily on privatisation to employees and will include between four and five million people.

It envisages that workers and pensioners of privatised firms be entitled to a dinar equivalent of 400 German marks ($225) in shares for each year of service. Farmers will enjoy the same right for each year of fully paid social service.
"We have to upgrade our fledgling trade and registration system, improve our software, so that we could do our business in an adequate way," Zecevic said.
Companies must first transform their status, shares must be divided and appear on the bourse and then they could be traded, she said.
The government sees 80 percent of around 5,000 small and medium-sized firms worth an estimated 100 billion marks being transformed in the next two years.
Economists fear that the majority of the new army of shareholders will not know what to do.
With an average wage of about 200 marks a month, many would probably just want to get rid of them to get any amount of money, analysts say.
But Zecevic said there was a growing interest of individuals in shares and trading.

"Individuals simply call in and try to find out about the conditions of the trade. Till now the capital market was almost completely dead, passive. But it seems people are starting to care about their property," she said.

Laws on securities and the stock exhange are more important for the bourse than privatisation itself, she said, adding: "But financial markets can be properly developed only after genuine privatisation."
The BSE, which also makes markets in financial instruments and commodities, did not trade equities in 1996.

The rules, set out by the Yugoslav Securities Commission last November with the aim of speeding up development of the local financial market, oblige banks and companies to sell part of their issued shares on the bourse if the issue is to qualify as successful.
This year, shares have sporadically appeared on the BSE but accounted for only four percent of some 1.2 billion dinars ($247 million) January-June turnover.
